why: A reading is not just a number. Where it came from decides what may be done with it, and a record that cannot tell a measured value from a typed one from a reported one is a record that will eventually be read wrongly by somebody in a hurry.

provenance.name: Measured by a device
provenance.detail: Read off a paired instrument and written straight into the record. The instrument, its serial and the date it was last calibrated travel with the reading.
provenance.trust: The strongest of the four, and only while the calibration is in date. An instrument out of calibration still produces a reading; what it stops producing is a reading anybody should act on without saying so.

provenance.name: Entered by a clinician
provenance.detail: Read off an instrument by a person and typed in, or taken by hand. Attributed to the registration of whoever typed it.
provenance.trust: As good as the person and the instrument they were holding. It is not weaker than a device reading — a manual blood pressure is a clinical skill — but it is a different fact and the record says which.

provenance.name: Reported by the patient
provenance.detail: What the person said, in the record as what they said rather than as a finding.
provenance.trust: Not a measurement. It is evidence about the person's experience, which is often the more useful thing, and it must never be presented as though a clinician observed it.

provenance.name: Calculated
provenance.detail: Computed from other readings — BMI from height and weight, a mean arterial pressure from a blood pressure.
provenance.trust: Exactly as good as its inputs, and it names them. A derived value whose inputs are unknown is not a value.

devices.name: Blood-pressure monitor
devices.note: Cuff size is a clinical decision the device cannot make. A reading taken on the wrong cuff is wrong in a direction nobody can correct for afterwards, so the cuff used is recorded with the reading.

devices.name: Pulse oximeter
devices.note: Reads high on dark skin under low perfusion. This is documented rather than corrected for, because the correction is not the platform's to invent.

devices.name: Infrared thermometer
devices.note: Site matters and is recorded: a forehead reading is not an oral one.

devices.name: Glucose meter
devices.note: Strips expire separately from the meter, and an expired strip reads low. The strip lot travels with the reading.

devices.name: Weighing scale
devices.note: Recorded with whether the patient was weighed standing, seated or in bed, because the three are not comparable.

devices.name: Single-lead ECG
devices.note: A single-lead trace is a screening tool. It is never a diagnosis, and any interpretation is decision support that a doctor signs or does not.

captureStates.name: Captured
captureStates.detail: Taken, and held on the device it was taken on. It exists nowhere else yet.

captureStates.name: Waiting to send
captureStates.detail: Finished and sealed, waiting for a connection. The nurse has done everything they can do.

captureStates.name: Sending
captureStates.detail: In flight. Interruptible without loss — an entry that does not land stays queued.

captureStates.name: Stored
captureStates.detail: Accepted by the server and in the record.

captureStates.name: Needs a decision
captureStates.detail: Landed against a record that already holds a reading for the same observation in the same visit. Nothing is merged and nothing is discarded.

captureStates.name: Refused
captureStates.detail: The server would not take it, and says why. It stays on the device until somebody decides what to do with it.

conflicts.name: Two readings, one observation
conflicts.detail: The same observation recorded twice in one visit — usually a retake after a doubtful first reading. Both are kept; a clinician says which stands, and the other stays visible as superseded rather than being deleted.

conflicts.name: The device clock disagrees
conflicts.detail: A device that has been offline may have drifted or been set by hand. The server's receipt time is authoritative for ordering; the device's time is kept beside it as what the device believed, never presented as the time it happened.

conflicts.name: The record moved on
conflicts.detail: The record changed while the entry was queued — a doctor has already signed, or the visit was cancelled. It is never applied silently after the fact.

conflicts.name: The capturer's standing lapsed
conflicts.detail: A nurse whose clearance lapsed between capture and sync. The reading was taken while she was cleared, so it is not discarded — but it is not filed on her authority alone either.

durability._note: What the offline queue survives, and what loses it — as data, per platform, because it was prose twice about the same disk. Android's FileBook carried three sentences about a JSON file in the app's private storage; iOS's CaptureQueueView and VisitQueueView carried six about a JSON file in Application Support; the web's queue screen carried one about a module-level array. A nurse reading the Android sentence and the iOS list would not have known they describe one behaviour, and nothing in this repository compared them. This section is that comparison. It does not flatten three platforms into one sentence: the web genuinely keeps less, because scripts/check-boundaries.mjs forbids the browser's local storage, session storage and IndexedDB across apps/web/src and a preview must not leave a patient's readings on a borrowed machine. What it does is make the promise one promise and the differences visible.
durability._promiseItServes: The rule this whole section exists under is rules.queuedIsNotLost above. It is not repeated here, and no store below may quietly mean something weaker by it.
durability._shape: Every store declares two things separately, and the difference between them is the point. `survives` and `lostTo` are what is true of the store — behaviour, in event ids, checkable across platforms. `says` is what a screen actually renders today, word for word. A store whose behaviour is wider than what it says is a screen with a gap in it, and holding both here is what makes the gap visible instead of invisible.

events.name: Reloading the page or closing the tab
A crash, a force-quit, or the process being killed
Clearing the app's storage from the operating system's settings

stores.where: A module-level array in the tab that is open. Nothing is written to the browser's storage, because nothing in apps/web/src may write to it.

lostTo: Closing this tab loses it. Nothing in this app may leave a patient’s readings on the machine it was opened on.

stores.why: The one platform that keeps less on purpose. A design preview opened on a borrowed laptop must not leave a patient's readings behind on it, so the store is deliberately the weakest of the three and the screen says so rather than implying a durability it has not got. What the contract asks for is owed here, not met.

stores.where: A JSON file in Application Support, written through FileManager with iOS data protection on it, and kept out of device backups.

survives: A crash or a force-quit. Every entry is written at the moment it is taken, not when the app closes.
A sign-out. This preview’s sign-out returns to the first-run flow and never touches the file — the entries belong to the work, not to the session.
lostTo: Deleting the app. iOS removes the file with it, and nothing here can prevent that.

Losing the phone. The file is deliberately kept out of device backups, because a queue of readings is special personal information and syncing it into somebody’s laptop backup is a disclosure nobody consented to. The answer to a lost phone is to send, not to back up.
A second device. Nothing is shared between phones; there is no server in this build to share it through.

stores.why: The readings a nurse has taken and not yet handed over. Excluded from device backups deliberately: readings are special personal information under POPIA and a phone syncing them into whatever backup it happens to be attached to is a disclosure nobody consented to. The cost is real — a lost phone loses the queue — and it is written down rather than assumed.

stores.where: The whole visit, in a file on this phone — not only the readings.

survives: A crash or a force-quit. Each piece is written the moment it is finished, not when the app closes.
A sign-out. This preview’s sign-out returns to the first-run flow and never touches the file — the work belongs to the visit, not to the session.
lostTo: Deleting the app. iOS removes the file with it, and nothing here can prevent that.

Losing the phone. The file is deliberately kept out of device backups: a consent, seven readings and a signature are special personal information, and syncing them into somebody’s laptop backup is a disclosure nobody consented to. The answer to a lost phone is to send, not to back up.
A second device. Nothing is shared between phones; there is no server in this build to share it through.

stores.why: The whole visit rather than only the readings: an identity check, a consent, the observations, what the nurse found and her sign-off. A record rewritten in the car from memory an hour later is a different record, which is a clinical safety problem before it is an inconvenience. Two files rather than one, because a parse failure in the readings must not take the assessment down with it.

stores.where: A file in this app’s own private storage on this phone. Nothing is sent anywhere: the app declares no permissions at all, internet included.

survives: Closing the app, the process being killed, a crash, restarting the phone, and signing out.
lostTo: Uninstalling MyThuso, clearing the app’s storage in Android settings, or a factory reset. It is never backed up off this phone — the manifest sets allowBackup to false.

stores.why: One FileBook serves both the reading ledger and the visit queue, one file per thing, so the machinery — the temporary file, the rename, the quarantine of anything that will not parse — is written once. Two events are on this list and not on the iOS ones because Android gives a person a button for them: storage can be cleared from settings without uninstalling. Two more are true here and are not in the sentence above — a lost phone and a second device lose this queue exactly as they lose the iOS one — and that gap between what is true and what the screen says is left visible here rather than papered over.

stores.where: Held in memory only, because this screen was opened without a file store.

survives: Nothing. Every entry here is lost when this screen closes.
lostTo: A crash, a restart, a sign-out, or leaving this screen.

stores.why: It says out loud that it keeps nothing. A preview store that stayed quiet about being a preview store is how a nurse comes to believe a promise the running app never made.

writeFailures._note: What happens when the disk will not take the work — as data, because these sentences were written into Android's FileBook and nowhere else, and the day iOS grows one it would have grown a fourth author. Three failures rather than one: a phone with no room left, a disk that refuses a write without saying why, and a file already written that will not read back. They are three because they leave three different things true. One sentence covering all three would send a nurse whose phone has plenty of room away to free space she does not need to free, and would tell a nurse whose ledger was quarantined that her work is not on the disk when it is, under another name.
writeFailures._shape: The same separation the stores above use, and it is the point of both. `leaves` is what is true after the failure, in outcome ids — behaviour, comparable between failures and checkable across platforms. `says` is the one sentence a screen renders, word for word. `saidBy` is which stores render it today, and it is deliberately not every store that can suffer the failure: iOS's two file queues can run a phone out of room exactly as Android's can, and neither of them says anything at all. That gap is left visible here rather than papered over, which is what holding both fields is for.
writeFailures._promiseItServes: rules.queuedIsNotLost, and its sibling in quarantinedFile below. Never dropped to make a sync succeed has to mean never dropped to make a write succeed and never dropped to make a parse succeed, so every failure here leaves nothing-deleted true and scripts/check-boundaries.mjs refuses one that does not.

outcomes.name: The work is still in memory and still on the screen
The work is not on the disk, so closing the app now loses it
Whatever was written down before this is untouched
Nothing is deleted or overwritten to get past it
The person holding the phone can do something that clears it
The file that would not read back is renamed aside and kept
What that file is now called is on the screen

failures.name: The phone has no room left
failures.detectedBy: The write threw, and the failure or one of the causes behind it named ENOSPC or said there was no space left on the device.
failures.says: This phone has no room left, so what you have just done could not be written down. It is still on the screen and it is still yours, but it is not on the disk: if the app closes now, it is gone. Free some space on the phone and it will be written again.
failures.why: The only write failure the person holding the phone can do anything about, which is the whole reason it is a failure of its own rather than a case of the one below it. It is also the only sentence here that ends in an instruction, and an instruction is honest only while it is the true cause.

failures.name: The disk would not take it, and did not say why
failures.detectedBy: The write threw for any other reason.
failures.says: This phone would not take the write, and it did not say why. What you have just done is still on the screen and still yours, but it is not on the disk: if the app closes now, it is gone. Nothing that was already written down has been touched.
failures.why: It differs from the one above by exactly one outcome, and that outcome is why there are two sentences instead of one. Telling a nurse whose phone has room to spare to go and free some sends her looking for a problem she has not got, and the next refusal she meets she will not read.

failures.name: What is on the disk will not read back
failures.detectedBy: The file exists and the parser would not take it. It is renamed aside before anything else is written to that name.
failures.why: Not a write failure at all, and it is in this list precisely so that it cannot be answered with a write failure's sentence. Nothing is on its way to the disk and nothing is waiting on the screen; what is at stake is work that was written down correctly and now cannot be read, and the answer to it is a rename rather than a retry. Its promise is quarantinedFile below rather than a sentence of its own, because a second wording of one promise is what this section exists to stop. What each screen adds to it is the new name, which is different on every phone and cannot be a shared literal — so new-name-on-screen is held as behaviour, against the files in namesTheFileIn, rather than as words.

quarantinedFile.sentence: A file that will not parse is kept, not deleted. Losing work to a bad parse is still losing work.
quarantinedFile.why: The sibling of queuedIsNotLost: never dropped to make a sync succeed has to mean never dropped to make a parse succeed either. The unreadable file is renamed aside and the screen says what it is now called, because a screen that says work was kept and cannot say where it was kept has asked to be believed rather than checked.

notEncrypted.sentence: None of this is encrypted by MyThuso. It is a design preview holding fictional readings in a file the operating system keeps private to the app, and no more than that.
notEncrypted.why: Real readings would need the controls in docs/PRIVACY-AND-SECURITY.md first. Said on the screen rather than implied by silence, because a queue that looks durable looks secure, and those are not the same claim.

rules.provenanceIsRequired: Every reading carries exactly one provenance. There is no default and no unknown: a value nobody can say the origin of is not filed.
rules.calibrationNeverRefuses: An out-of-date calibration marks a reading, it does not block it. A nurse in a home with one instrument still needs the number; what she must not have is the number without the caveat.
rules.deviceClockIsNotTruth: The device's own time is recorded as what the device believed. Ordering uses the server's receipt time.
rules.conflictsAreNotMerged: Nothing is auto-merged and nothing is auto-discarded. A timestamp does not win a clinical disagreement; a clinician does.
rules.queuedIsNotLost: An entry that has been captured is the nurse's work. It survives a crash, a restart and a sign-out, and it is never dropped to make a sync succeed.
rules.offlineNeverServesStaleSilently: A value read from the device's own store carries when it was written, on screen, in words.
